LLM conceptual structure from verified feature lists aligns moderately well with human feature norms (squared Procrustes correlation 0.89), but other LLM-derived embeddings align less well.
Chain-of-thought prompting improves alignment with human conceptual structure for some models but does not achieve human-level coherence.
Embeddings from internal representations (e.g., GPT-3 hidden layers, word2vec, CLIP) do not cohere well with each other or with human embeddings.
papers.limitation:
The study uses a constrained set of 30 concepts from two domains; a larger scale study might reveal different results.
The LLM simulations did not employ advanced prompting techniques like tree-of-thought or self-consistency, which might improve coherence.
LLMs lack multimodal sensory experience that humans have, which might affect conceptual organization.
future_direction: Conduct a larger scale study on larger concept sets.
Investigate the use of advanced prompting techniques (e.g., tree-of-thought, self-consistency) to improve conceptual coherence in LLMs.
papers.abstract: Neural network models of language have long been used as a tool for developing hypotheses about conceptual representation in the mind and brain. For many years, such use involved extracting vector-space representations of words and using distances among these to predict or understand human behavior in various semantic tasks. Contemporary large language models (LLMs), however, make it possible to interrogate the latent structure of conceptual representations using experimental methods nearly identical to those commonly used with human participants. The current work utilizes three common techniques borrowed from cognitive psychology to estimate and compare the structure of concepts in humans and a suite of LLMs. In humans, we show that conceptual structure is robust to differences in culture, language, and method of estimation. Structures estimated from LLM behavior, while individually fairly consistent with those estimated from human behavior, vary much more depending upon the particular task used to generate responses--across tasks, estimates of conceptual structure from the very same model cohere less with one another than do human structure estimates. These results highlight an important difference between contemporary LLMs and human cognition, with implications for understanding some fundamental limitations of contemporary machine language.

papers.title: Examining the Inductive Bias of Neural Language Models with Artificial\n Languages
papers.research_question: What are the inductive biases of neural language models with respect to typological features such as word order, and do these biases reflect tendencies in attested natural languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel method using artificial languages to investigate inductive biases of language models in a controlled causal framework, and finds that transformers and LSTMs exhibit different inductive biases regarding word order, with transformers showing clear preferences and LSTMs showing little preference.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel methodology using carefully controlled artificial languages to study inductive biases, finding that LSTMs and transformers have starkly different inductive biases with respect to word order, with LSTMs showing little variation and transformers showing significant variation across languages.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based language models show little preference for any particular word ordering across the artificial languages.
Transformer-based language models show clear preferences for some word orderings over others.
The inductive biases of neither LSTM nor transformer architectures reflect tendencies observed in attested natural languages (e.g., transformers perform similarly on common SOV and rare OVS orders).
The proposed method of using artificial languages allows for controlled causal claims about the effect of typological features on model performance.
Mixed-effects modeling reveals specific interaction effects between typological switches for transformers, but not for LSTMs.
papers.limitation: The artificial grammars are simple and do not cover all possible constructions found in natural languages.
future_direction: Extending the base grammars to test additional hypotheses.
Exploring automated methods for assigning weights to grammar productions.
papers.abstract:
Since language models are used to model a wide variety of languages, it is
natural to ask whether the neural architectures used for the task have
inductive biases towards modeling particular types of languages. Investigation
of these biases has proved complicated due to the many variables that appear in
the experimental setup. Languages vary in many typological dimensions, and it
is difficult to single out one or two to investigate without the others acting
as confounders. We propose a novel method for investigating the inductive
biases of language models using artificial languages. These languages are
constructed to allow us to create parallel corpora across languages that differ
only in the typological feature being investigated, such as word order. We then
use them to train and test language models. This constitutes a fully controlled
causal framework, and demonstrates how grammar engineering can serve as a
useful tool for analyzing neural models. Using this method, we find that
commonly used neural architectures exhibit different inductive biases: LSTMs
display little preference with respect to word ordering, while transformers
display a clear preference for some orderings over others. Further, we find
that neither the inductive bias of the LSTM nor that of the transformer appears
to reflect any tendencies that we see in attested natural languages.

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: Language Models Encode Numbers Using Digit Representations in Base 10
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally represent numbers? Specifically, do they use digit-wise representations in base 10 rather than a linear value space?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs internally represent numbers using individual circular representations per-digit in base 10, which explains their error patterns on numerical tasks.
papers.conclusion: Circular digit-wise probes can effectively extract number representations in base 10, and editing these representations can alter model generation, suggesting digit-wise representations are used for arithmetic.
papers.key_findings:
LLM errors on numerical tasks are often scattered across the digits of the answer rather than normally distributed around its numeric value.
Probes can accurately recover digit values in base 10 from hidden representations, but not the whole number value directly.
Causal interventions on digit representations can modify the number accordingly, confirming the causal significance of digit-wise representations.
The digit-wise representation is base-10 specific, with high accuracy for base 10 probes compared to other bases.
This representation holds across models with different tokenization schemes, such as Llama 3 8B and Mistral 7B.
papers.limitation:
The study does not conclusively show that digit-wise representation is the only representation of numeracy in LLMs; there may be superposition of multiple redundant representations.
The focus is exclusively on natural numbers, leaving fractions and other numeric values for future work.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to fractions and other numeric values beyond natural numbers.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) frequently make errors when handling even simple numerical problems, such as comparing two small numbers. A natural hypothesis is that these errors stem from how LLMs represent numbers, and specifically, whether their representations of numbers capture their numeric values. We tackle this question from the observation that LLM errors on numerical tasks are often distributed across the digits of the answer rather than normally around its numeric value. Through a series of probing experiments and causal interventions, we show that LLMs internally represent numbers with individual circular representations per-digit in base 10. This digit-wise representation, as opposed to a value representation, sheds light on the error patterns of models on tasks involving numerical reasoning and could serve as a basis for future studies on analyzing numerical mechanisms in LLMs.

papers.title: Are Pretrained Language Models Symbolic Reasoners over Knowledge?
papers.research_question: How do pretrained language models learn factual knowledge? Specifically, can they perform symbolic reasoning to infer unseen facts, and what factors affect memorization of facts?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that PLMs can learn some one-hop symbolic reasoning rules but overgeneralize, struggle with two-hop reasoning, and that memorization is influenced by frequency and schema conformity.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that BERT can to some extent infer facts not explicitly seen during training via symbolic rules, and effective knowledge acquisition combines memorization and symbolic reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
BERT can learn one-hop rules like equivalence and implication, but overgeneralizes symmetry and inversion.
BERT struggles with two-hop reasoning (composition) unless provided with richer semantic context (schema).
BERT does not learn a general concept of negation; it relies on co-occurrences.
Memorization is successful for frequent facts and schema-conformant facts; exceptions are harder to memorize unless repeated.
When memory capacity is limited, schema-conformant facts and exceptions compete based on frequency.
papers.limitation:
Variation in generated data is more limited than in naturally occurring data.
Semantics are deliberately restricted to one rule only per generated corpus.
We do not investigate effects of model and corpus size.
future_direction: Relax the simplifying assumptions made in the study.
Improve PLMs' ability to learn symbolic rules by imposing additional inductive biases on architectures or modifying training corpora.
papers.abstract: How can pretrained language models (PLMs) learn factual knowledge from the training set? We investigate the two most important mechanisms: reasoning and memorization. Prior work has attempted to quantify the number of facts PLMs learn, but we present, using synthetic data, the first study that investigates the causal relation between facts present in training and facts learned by the PLM. For reasoning, we show that PLMs seem to learn to apply some symbolic reasoning rules correctly but struggle with others, including two-hop reasoning. Further analysis suggests that even the application of learned reasoning rules is flawed. For memorization, we identify schema conformity (facts systematically supported by other facts) and frequency as key factors for its success.

papers.title: When classifying grammatical role, BERT doesn't care about word order...\n except when it matters
papers.research_question: How do BERT and GPT-2 represent grammatical role (subject vs. object), and is this representation sensitive to word order, especially in sentences where lexical semantics are insufficient?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that while early layer embeddings in BERT and GPT-2 are dominated by lexical semantics, word order becomes crucial in later layers for representing grammatical role in non-prototypical sentences, allowing models to override lexical cues.
papers.conclusion: Considering non-prototypical instances is crucial for understanding how language models represent language, as the combinatorial power of syntax is most evident when expressing surprising or impossible meanings.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantics dominates early layer representations, while grammatical information is gradually acquired in later layers for non-prototypical sentences.
Models learn to represent the effect of syntactic word order on meaning independently from distributional information, as shown by accurate classification on argument-swapped sentences.
General positional information (e.g., primacy) is insufficient for grammatical role classification in non-prototypical cases; fine-grained syntactic word order is necessary.
Probing on average (prototypical) sentences obscures the gradual acquisition of syntactic information, which is only visible when analyzing non-prototypical cases.
The ability to understand non-prototypical meanings, a hallmark of human language, is present in the models' later-layer representations.
papers.abstract:
Because meaning can often be inferred from lexical semantics alone, word
order is often a redundant cue in natural language. For example, the words
chopped, chef, and onion are more likely used to convey "The chef chopped the
onion," not "The onion chopped the chef." Recent work has shown large language
models to be surprisingly word order invariant, but crucially has largely
considered natural prototypical inputs, where compositional meaning mostly
matches lexical expectations. To overcome this confound, we probe grammatical
role representation in English BERT and GPT-2, on instances where lexical
expectations are not sufficient, and word order knowledge is necessary for
correct classification. Such non-prototypical instances are naturally occurring
English sentences with inanimate subjects or animate objects, or sentences
where we systematically swap the arguments to make sentences like "The onion
chopped the chef". We find that, while early layer embeddings are largely
lexical, word order is in fact crucial in defining the later-layer
representations of words in semantically non-prototypical positions. Our
experiments isolate the effect of word order on the contextualization process,
and highlight how models use context in the uncommon, but critical, instances
where it matters.

papers.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
papers.research_question: Can transformers learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge, and how does grokking enable this? What are the differences in systematic generalization between composition and comparison tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can learn implicit reasoning over parametric knowledge through grokking, but systematic generalization varies: composition fails out-of-distribution while comparison succeeds. Mechanistic analysis reveals the formation of generalizing circuits and explains the differences, guiding data and training setups and suggesting architectural improvements.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are capable of learning implicit reasoning through grokking, but the level of systematic generalization depends on the task and the circuit configuration. The findings guide data and training setups and suggest improvements to the transformer architecture for better cross-layer memory sharing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can learn implicit reasoning only through grokking (extended training far beyond overfitting).
The speed of grokking correlates with the ratio of inferred to atomic facts (data distribution), not the absolute training data size.
For composition, transformers fail to generalize systematically to out-of-distribution examples, while for comparison, they succeed.
Mechanistic analysis reveals distinct generalizing circuits: for composition, a sequential circuit that stores atomic facts in separate layers; for comparison, a parallel circuit that stores atomic facts in the same layer.
In a complex reasoning task with a large search space, a fully grokked transformer achieves near-perfect accuracy, while state-of-the-art LLMs with non-parametric memory (GPT-4-Turbo, Gemini-1.5-Pro) fail regardless of prompting or retrieval augmentation.
papers.limitation:
The task formulation (induction and application of inference rules from atomic and inferred facts) may not apply to the full spectrum of reasoning types.
The study is limited to synthetic tasks and may not fully capture real-world reasoning complexities.
future_direction: Developing cross-layer memory-sharing mechanisms for transformers (e.g., memory-augmentation, explicit recurrence) to improve systematic generalization.
Investigating the tradeoff between parametric and non-parametric memory in language models.
Understanding the role of verbalizations (e.g., chain-of-thought) in teaching models to reason implicitly.
papers.abstract: We study whether transformers can learn to implicitly reason over parametric knowledge, a skill that even the most capable language models struggle with. Focusing on two representative reasoning types, composition and comparison, we consistently find that transformers can learn implicit reasoning, but only through grokking, i.e., extended training far beyond overfitting. The levels of generalization also vary across reasoning types: when faced with out-of-distribution examples, transformers fail to systematically generalize for composition but succeed for comparison. We delve into the model's internals throughout training, conducting analytical experiments that reveal: 1) the mechanism behind grokking, such as the formation of the generalizing circuit and its relation to the relative efficiency of generalizing and memorizing circuits, and 2) the connection between systematicity and the configuration of the generalizing circuit. Our findings guide data and training setup to better induce implicit reasoning and suggest potential improvements to the transformer architecture, such as encouraging cross-layer knowledge sharing. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for a challenging reasoning task with a large search space, GPT-4-Turbo and Gemini-1.5-Pro based on non-parametric memory fail badly regardless of prompting styles or retrieval augmentation, while a fully grokked transformer can achieve near-perfect accuracy, showcasing the power of parametric memory for complex reasoning.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models encode and apply high-level relational concepts for analogical reasoning, and how do they structurally align analogous situations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper investigates the internal mechanisms of analogical reasoning in LLMs, finding that they encode relational information in mid-upper layers but struggle to apply it, and that successful reasoning is associated with strong structural alignment between analogous situations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs show emerging but limited capabilities in analogical reasoning, with parallels to human cognition in encoding relational information and structural alignment, but gaps in application and alignment.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs effectively encode underlying relationships between analogous entities in mid-upper layers, with relational information being a key factor for correct reasoning.
LLMs struggle not only when relational information is missing but also when attempting to apply it to new entities.
Strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer and improve performance.
Successful analogical reasoning is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, while failures show degraded alignment.
Analogical structure becomes linearly separable in middle layers, and token-level alignment (measured by Mutual Alignment Score) is higher for correct analogies.
future_direction: Future research into understanding and improving the analogical reasoning capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: Analogical reasoning is at the core of human cognition, serving as an important foundation for a variety of intellectual activities. While prior work has shown that LLMs can represent task patterns and surface-level concepts, it remains unclear whether these models can encode high-level relational concepts and apply them to novel situations through structured comparisons. In this work, we explore this fundamental aspect using proportional and story analogies, and identify three key findings. First, LLMs effectively encode the underlying relationships between analogous entities; both attributive and relational information propagate through mid-upper layers in correct cases, whereas reasoning failures reflect missing relational information within these layers. Second, unlike humans, LLMs often struggle not only when relational information is missing, but also when attempting to apply it to new entities. In such cases, strategically patching hidden representations at critical token positions can facilitate information transfer to a certain extent. Lastly, successful analogical reasoning in LLMs is marked by strong structural alignment between analogous situations, whereas failures often reflect degraded or misplaced alignment. Overall, our findings reveal that LLMs exhibit emerging but limited capabilities in encoding and applying high-level relational concepts, highlighting both parallels and gaps with human cognition.

papers.title: Word Order Does Matter and Shuffled Language Models Know It
papers.research_question: Do shuffled language models still have traces of word order information? Why is there a gap in performance between models without position embeddings and models trained on shuffled tokens? Are there NLU benchmarks, other than GLUE, on which shuffled language models perform poorly?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that language models trained on shuffled text retain word order information due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and correlations between sentence length and content, and that some NLU tasks are sensitive to word order.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that models trained on shuffled text retain word order knowledge, largely at the local level, due to cues like adjacent BPE symbols and sentence length correlations. The order of shuffling (before/after BPE) influences this acquisition, and some NLU tasks are highly sensitive to word order.
papers.key_findings:
Shuffled language models contain word order information, as shown by probing tasks.
The performance gap between models without position embeddings and shuffled models is due to position embeddings providing inductive bias and the presence of n-grams when shuffling before BPE segmentation.
Even when shuffling after segmentation, models retain some word order information due to statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities.
Attention patterns in shuffled models show a bias towards adjacent tokens.
Some NLU tasks (e.g., Winograd Schema, ReCoRD) require word order information and show significant performance drops for shuffled models.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have shown that language models pretrained and/or fine-tuned on randomly permuted sentences exhibit competitive performance on GLUE, putting into question the importance of word order information. Somewhat counter-intuitively, some of these studies also report that position embeddings appear to be crucial for models' good performance with shuffled text. We probe these language models for word order information and investigate what position embeddings learned from shuffled text encode, showing that these models retain information pertaining to the original, naturalistic word order. We show this is in part due to a subtlety in how shuffling is implemented in previous work -before rather than after subword segmentation. Surprisingly, we find even Language models trained on text shuffled after subword segmentation retain some semblance of information about word order because of the statistical dependencies between sentence length and unigram probabilities. Finally, we show that beyond GLUE, a variety of language understanding tasks do require word order information, often to an extent that cannot be learned through fine-tuning. * Equal contribution. Order was decided by a coin toss.

papers.title: Language Models with Rationality
papers.research_question: How can we make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit and resolve inconsistencies so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent belief system?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REFLEX, a new system architecture that adds a rational layer on top of an LLM to construct explicit belief graphs and resolve inconsistencies, improving belief consistency without harming answer accuracy.
papers.conclusion: REFLEX is an important step towards improving confidence in system behavior and towards trustable deployment of LLMs in practical applications by providing interpretable reasoning and repairing latent inconsistencies.
papers.key_findings:
REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy.
The rational layer provides faithful explanations by supporting answers with interpretable chains of reasoning from a consistent belief system.
The constraint reasoner can correct initially wrong answers, correct erroneous latent model beliefs, and identify and reject bad rules.
All three types of rules (p → h, XOR, MC) contribute to the system's consistency improvements.
Failure modes include missing rules, incorrect beliefs, incorrect rules, ambiguous statements, and multiple valid answers.
papers.limitation:
The reasoning component can make mistakes, resulting in the overall system rejecting true statements or accepting false ones.
The method is evaluated only on a T5-11B based LLM; effectiveness with newer and larger LLMs like ChatGPT and LLaMA remains to be evaluated.
No formal user study has been conducted to measure the value of belief graphs for providing explanations and gaining user trust.
future_direction: Incorporating the question's context in the belief statements to make semantics more precise and avoid ambiguity.
Using the belief graph to identify uncertain reasoning pieces and guide a human-in-the-loop mechanism for correction or validation.
Maintaining a persistent belief graph over multiple questions to make the system more consistent across questions in a dialog setting.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) are proficient at question-answering (QA), it is not always clear how (or even if) an answer follows from their latent "beliefs". This lack of interpretability is a growing impediment to widespread use of LLMs. To address this, our goals are to make model beliefs and their inferential relationships explicit, and to resolve inconsistencies that may exist, so that answers are supported by interpretable chains of reasoning drawn from a consistent network of beliefs. Our approach, which we call REFLEX, is to add a rational, self-reflecting layer on top of the LLM. First, given a question, we construct a belief graph using a backward-chaining process to materialize relevant model beliefs (including beliefs about answer candidates) and their inferential relationships. Second, we identify and minimize contradictions in that graph using a formal constraint reasoner. We find that REFLEX significantly improves consistency (by 8%-11% absolute) without harming overall answer accuracy, resulting in answers supported by faithful chains of reasoning drawn from a more consistent belief system. This suggests a new style of system architecture in which an LLM extended with a rational layer can provide an interpretable window into system beliefs, add a systematic reasoning capability, and repair latent inconsistencies present in the LLM.

papers.title: Characterizing the Role of Similarity in the Property Inferences of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do language models perform property inheritance, and what roles do taxonomic relations and categorical similarities play in this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Language models' property inheritance behavior is jointly explained by taxonomic relations and categorical similarity, and these features are entangled in the model's internal representations.
papers.conclusion: LMs perform property inheritance with sensitivity to both taxonomic relations and similarity, and these two factors are entangled in their internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
LMs show high taxonomic sensitivity in property inheritance, but also positive correlation with similarity between categories.
LMs are more likely to extend a property when categories are taxonomically related and highly similar.
Causal analysis reveals that the subspaces responsible for property inheritance reflect both taxonomic and similarity features.
Taxonomy and similarity are fundamentally entangled in LM representations, even when trained on unambiguous taxonomic data.
LMs exhibit graded property inheritance behavior similar to humans, influenced by similarity.
papers.limitation:
Alternative similarities could have been used, such as WordNet similarities or LM-derived similarities.
The study focuses only on concrete object noun concepts, not abstract or ad-hoc concepts.
The work does not engage with knowledge editing, which could be an interesting extension.
Property inheritance is only one type of inductive problem; broader generalization is not studied.
Similarity in inductive problems can be context-sensitive, which is not accounted for with nonce properties.
future_direction: Exploring other similarity measures and their correlation with property inheritance.
Extending the investigation to abstract and ad-hoc concepts.
Testing the entanglement of taxonomy and similarity in human property inheritance.
papers.abstract: Property inheritance -- a phenomenon where novel properties are projected from higher level categories (e.g., birds) to lower level ones (e.g., sparrows) -- provides a unique window into how humans organize and deploy conceptual knowledge. It is debated whether this ability arises due to explicitly stored taxonomic knowledge vs. simple computations of similarity between mental representations. How are these mechanistic hypotheses manifested in contemporary language models? In this work, we investigate how LMs perform property inheritance with behavioral and causal representational analysis experiments. We find that taxonomy and categorical similarities are not mutually exclusive in LMs' property inheritance behavior. That is, LMs are more likely to project novel properties from one category to the other when they are taxonomically related and at the same time, highly similar. Our findings provide insight into the conceptual structure of language models and may suggest new psycholinguistic experiments for human subjects.

papers.title: Attention Satisfies: A Constraint-Satisfaction Lens on Factual Errors of Language Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) internally behave when they generate factually incorrect text, and can attention to constraint tokens predict factual errors?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a strong positive relationship between an LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of its generations. It proposes SAT Probe, a method that probes attention patterns to predict factual errors and constraint satisfaction.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that attention patterns in LLMs provide a reliable signal for predicting factual errors, contributing to the mechanistic understanding of LLMs and offering a pathway to enhance their reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Attention to constraint tokens strongly correlates with the factual correctness of LLM generations.
SAT Probe, a linear probe on attention weights, can predict factual errors comparably to the model's own confidence score.
Larger LLMs tend to pay more attention to constraint tokens and achieve higher factual accuracy.
The total attention contribution from constraints across layers can be used to predict LLM success on factual queries.
Attention patterns can be used for early error identification, potentially stopping costly generation early.
papers.limitation: Exact match is used as a strict verification criterion for single-constraint queries, which could introduce noise to evaluations.
papers.abstract: We investigate the internal behavior of Transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) when they generate factually incorrect text. We propose modeling factual queries as constraint satisfaction problems and use this framework to investigate how the LLM interacts internally with factual constraints. We find a strong positive relationship between the LLM's attention to constraint tokens and the factual accuracy of generations. We curate a suite of 10 datasets containing over 40,000 prompts to study the task of predicting factual errors with the Llama-2 family across all scales (7B, 13B, 70B). We propose SAT Probe, a method probing attention patterns, that can predict factual errors and fine-grained constraint satisfaction, and allow early error identification. The approach and findings take another step towards using the mechanistic understanding of LLMs to enhance their reliability.

papers.title: Editing Common Sense in Transformers
papers.research_question: Whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and if so, can model editing effectively repair incorrect commonsense plausibility judgments?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates strong causal relations between commonsense plausibility judgments and early MLP layers in Transformers, and introduces MEMIT_CSK, an improved model editing method for commonsense that outperforms fine-tuning baselines.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that commonsense knowledge is localized in early MLP layers and can be effectively edited with MEMIT_CSK, providing a compelling direction for incorporating commonsense feedback into transformers through direct model editing.
papers.key_findings:
High task performance is crucial for achieving strong causal tracing results.
Targeted part of speech and layer locations affect causal tracing conclusions and edit success.
MEMIT_CSK exhibits configuration generalization (hyperparameters transfer well to unseen data).
MEMIT_CSK exhibits semantic generalization (balances affected and unaffected neighborhoods).
MEMIT_CSK outperforms fine-tuning for repairing commonsense knowledge.
papers.limitation:
Unable to investigate larger open-sourced models like GPT-J and GPT-NeoX due to resource limitations.
Focus on the binary plausibility prediction task, while parameter editing could improve models on various commonsense tasks.
The optimal edit token (subject, verb, or object) varies among datasets; a single generalized optimal edit token requires further investigation.
future_direction: Investigating the research questions on larger models.
Extending parameter editing to improve models on various commonsense tasks.
Further investigation into the existence of a single generalized optimal edit token.
papers.abstract: Editing model parameters directly in Transformers makes updating open-source transformer-based models possible without re-training (Meng et al., 2023). However, these editing methods have only been evaluated on statements about encyclopedic knowledge with a single correct answer. Commonsense knowledge with multiple correct answers, e.g., an apple can be green or red but not transparent, has not been studied but is as essential for enhancing transformers' reliability and usefulness. In this paper, we investigate whether commonsense judgments are causally associated with localized, editable parameters in Transformers, and we provide an affirmative answer. We find that directly applying the MEMIT editing algorithm results in sub-par performance and improve it for the commonsense domain by varying edit tokens and improving the layer selection strategy, i.e., $MEMIT_{CSK}$. GPT-2 Large and XL models edited using $MEMIT_{CSK}$ outperform best-fine-tuned baselines by 10.97% and 10.73% F1 scores on PEP3k and 20Q datasets. In addition, we propose a novel evaluation dataset, PROBE SET, that contains unaffected and affected neighborhoods, affected paraphrases, and affected reasoning challenges. $MEMIT_{CSK}$ performs well across the metrics while fine-tuning baselines show significant trade-offs between unaffected and affected metrics. These results suggest a compelling future direction for incorporating feedback about common sense into Transformers through direct model editing.

papers.title: The better your Syntax, the better your Semantics? Probing Pretrained Language Models for the English Comparative Correlative
papers.research_question: Are pretrained language models (PLMs) able to recognize the syntactic structure and understand the semantic meaning of the English comparative correlative construction?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that PLMs can recognize the syntactic structure of the English comparative correlative but fail to understand its semantic meaning, indicating substantial shortcomings in linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: PLMs are able to recognize the comparative correlative syntactically but fail to understand its meaning, indicating that PLMs still suffer from substantial shortcomings in central domains of linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
PLMs can distinguish positive and negative instances of the comparative correlative in syntactic probing tasks.
PLMs fail to understand the semantics of the comparative correlative, performing at chance level in semantic application tasks.
Models are highly susceptible to biases such as recency and lexical identity, which obscure any underlying semantic knowledge.
Calibration methods do not improve semantic performance above chance level.
The findings suggest that PLMs still lack deep semantic understanding of linguistic constructions despite their syntactic capabilities.
papers.limitation:
The semantic task only provides a lower bound for understanding; success does not guarantee full comprehension.
The synthetic data used for syntactic probing only covers one specific subtype of the comparative correlative.
Models might not have seen enough examples of the construction or lack the necessary meaning representation to learn its semantics.
future_direction: Extend the probing approach to other constructions in construction grammar.
Investigate why models fail to learn the semantics of the comparative correlative and explore ways to improve semantic understanding.
Explore the compatibility of construction grammar with the learning processes of PLMs.
papers.abstract: Construction Grammar (CxG) is a paradigm from cognitive linguistics emphasising the connection between syntax and semantics. Rather than rules that operate on lexical items, it posits constructions as the central building blocks of language, i.e., linguistic units of different granularity that combine syntax and semantics. As a first step towards assessing the compatibility of CxG with the syntactic and semantic knowledge demonstrated by state-of-the-art pretrained language models (PLMs), we present an investigation of their capability to classify and understand one of the most commonly studied constructions, the English comparative correlative (CC). We conduct experiments examining the classification accuracy of a syntactic probe on the one hand and the models’ behaviour in a semantic application task on the other, with BERT, RoBERTa, and DeBERTa as the example PLMs. Our results show that all three investigated PLMs are able to recognise the structure of the CC but fail to use its meaning. While human-like performance of PLMs on many NLP tasks has been alleged, this indicates that PLMs still suffer from substantial shortcomings in central domains of linguistic knowledge.

papers.title: Is Bigger and Deeper Always Better? Probing LLaMA Across Scales and Layers
papers.research_question: Does increasing model size and depth improve LLaMA's intrinsic understanding and advanced capabilities like reasoning and calculation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that increasing model size does not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess but can enhance reasoning abilities and reduce hallucinations beyond certain thresholds. Also, lower layers lack arithmetic and factual knowledge but possess logical thinking and multilingual abilities, while top layers house computational power and real-world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Beyond generation, the study uses probing tasks to reveal that LLaMA models have nearly identical computational abilities and factual knowledge regardless of scale, while increasing size benefits reasoning. Lower layers contain multilingual features and reasoning abilities but lack computational skills and real-world knowledge, which are housed in the top layers.
papers.key_findings:
Horizontally, enlarging model sizes almost could not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess. Instead, it can enhance reasoning abilities, especially in math problem solving, and helps reduce hallucinations, but only beyond certain size thresholds.
Vertically, the lower layers of LLaMA lack substantial arithmetic and factual knowledge, showcasing logical thinking, multilingual and recognitive abilities, with top layers housing most computational power and real-world knowledge.
The optimal performance in math problem solving and computational abilities is not always at the final layer, but often in several layers before the last. For factual knowledge, the final layer is crucial.
In cross-lingual reasoning, performance decreases as layers deepen, indicating that earlier layers preserve multilingual features.
Lower layers across different model scales show similar abilities.
papers.limitation:
Why LLaMA obtains optimal performances in their last 2-7 layers rather than the absolute final layer in some tasks like computation?
Why the penultimate layer of LLaMA performs much better than the last layer in cross-lingual math problem solving tasks?
Why essentially all LLaMA models begin to show significant performance improvements starting from their mid-layer networks?
papers.abstract: This paper presents an in-depth analysis of Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on LLaMA, a prominent open-source foundational model in natural language processing. Instead of assessing LLaMA through its generative output, we design multiple-choice tasks to probe its intrinsic understanding in high-order tasks such as reasoning and computation. We examine the model horizontally, comparing different sizes, and vertically, assessing different layers. We unveil several key and uncommon findings based on the designed probing tasks: (1) Horizontally, enlarging model sizes almost could not automatically impart additional knowledge or computational prowess. Instead, it can enhance reasoning abilities, especially in math problem solving, and helps reduce hallucinations, but only beyond certain size thresholds; (2) In vertical analysis, the lower layers of LLaMA lack substantial arithmetic and factual knowledge, showcasing logical thinking, multilingual and recognitive abilities, with top layers housing most computational power and real-world knowledge.

papers.title: Inspecting and Editing Knowledge Representations in Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we map natural language statements to fact encodings in an LM's internal representations to enable editing and probing of knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: REMEDI is a method that learns to map natural language statements to fact encodings in LM representations, enabling both editing of knowledge (by adding vectors to hidden representations) and probing of existing knowledge.
papers.conclusion: REMEDI links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.
papers.key_findings:
REMEDI can patch errors made by an LM and insert new facts with or without context provided in the prompt.
REMEDI can help detect errors before generation by comparing edit vectors to unedited representations.
REMEDI increases accuracy on occupation classification and factual editing tasks compared to prompting baselines.
REMEDI generalizes from out-of-context training to in-context editing, suggesting unified representation of background and contextual knowledge.
REMEDI edits preserve correlations between features (e.g., adding 'made of metal' increases probability of 'shiny').
papers.limitation:
REMEDI can occasionally lead to disfluent or incorrect generations.
REMEDI sometimes damages the essence of the entity (e.g., making Wiener schnitzel an anime instead of a food).
REMEDI can also cause unrelated facts to change (e.g., changing the air dates of a TV show).
future_direction: Developing controlled generation interfaces that allow direct steering of model behavior in representation space.
Building tools for monitoring and controlling language generation by directly specifying facts and situations in an LM's native encoding scheme.
papers.abstract: Neural language models (LMs) represent facts about the world described by text. Sometimes these facts derive from training data (in most LMs, a representation of the word "banana" encodes the fact that bananas are fruits). Sometimes facts derive from input text itself (a representation of the sentence "I poured out the bottle" encodes the fact that the bottle became empty). We describe REMEDI, a method for learning to map statements in natural language to fact encodings in an LM's internal representation system. REMEDI encodings can be used as knowledge editors: when added to LM hidden representations, they modify downstream generation to be consistent with new facts. REMEDI encodings may also be used as probes: when compared to LM representations, they reveal which properties LMs already attribute to mentioned entities, in some cases making it possible to predict when LMs will generate outputs that conflict with background knowledge or input text. REMEDI thus links work on probing, prompting, and LM editing, and offers steps toward general tools for fine-grained inspection and control of knowledge in LMs.

papers.title: Reasoning in Large Language Models: A Geometric Perspective
papers.research_question: How does the geometric structure of LLMs, specifically the density of self-attention graphs and intrinsic dimension, correlate with their reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper establishes that the density of self-attention graphs defines the intrinsic dimension of MLP inputs, and higher intrinsic dimension correlates with improved reasoning capabilities in LLMs, providing a geometric framework for understanding reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The geometric properties of LLMs, such as input space partitioning and intrinsic dimension, are crucial for reasoning capabilities, suggesting avenues for improving smaller models.
papers.key_findings:
Higher density of self-attention graphs increases the intrinsic dimension of inputs to MLP blocks.
Increased intrinsic dimension leads to more regions in MLP input space, enhancing expressive power.
Empirical evidence shows that higher intrinsic dimension at the final layer correlates with better reasoning performance.
Context length and number of attention heads can increase intrinsic dimension without modifying model weights.
Random tokens increase intrinsic dimension at first layers but not at final layers, and do not improve reasoning.
papers.limitation:
The study presents a limited set of experiments and requires further exploration.
Approximation power is not equivalent to generalization, and this connection is not fully explored.
future_direction: Further exploration of the phenomenon to enhance reasoning capabilities.
Investigating how geometric insights relate to the generalization capabilities of LLMs.
papers.abstract: The advancement of large language models (LLMs) for real-world applications hinges critically on enhancing their reasoning capabilities. In this work, we explore the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs) through their geometrical understanding. We establish a connection between the expressive power of LLMs and the density of their self-attention graphs. Our analysis demonstrates that the density of these graphs defines the intrinsic dimension of the inputs to the MLP blocks. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis and toy examples that a higher intrinsic dimension implies a greater expressive capacity of the LLM. We further provide empirical evidence linking this geometric framework to recent advancements in methods aimed at enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs.

papers.title: Delving into the Reversal Curse: How Far Can Large Language Models Generalize?
papers.research_question: How does the reversal curse manifest across various tasks, and what are the underlying generalization abilities and problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that the reversal curse is more likely a backward recall deficiency, and identifies an inherent 'thinking bias' in LLMs where they preferentially use names to initiate fact recall, which strongly influences their generalization ability based on training data structure.
papers.conclusion: The reversal curse is a backward recall deficiency in decoder-only models, and LLMs' inherent thinking bias underscores the critical importance of appropriate training data structure for successful knowledge application and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs can generalize to 'B is A' when both A and B are presented in context (e.g., in multiple-choice questions).
Generalization ability is highly correlated with the structure of training documents (works for '[Name] is [Description]' but not the reverse).
LLMs possess an inherent thinking bias: they consistently start fact recall with names provided in the query.
The negative impact of this bias on downstream task performance is hard to mitigate through training alone.
papers.abstract: While large language models (LLMs) showcase unprecedented capabilities, they also exhibit certain inherent limitations when facing seemingly trivial tasks. A prime example is the recently debated "reversal curse", which surfaces when models, having been trained on the fact "A is B", struggle to generalize this knowledge to infer that "B is A". In this paper, we examine the manifestation of the reversal curse across various tasks and delve into both the generalization abilities and the problem-solving mechanisms of LLMs. This investigation leads to a series of significant insights: (1) LLMs are able to generalize to "B is A" when both A and B are presented in the context as in the case of a multiple-choice question. (2) This generalization ability is highly correlated to the structure of the fact "A is B" in the training documents. For example, this generalization only applies to biographies structured in "[Name] is [Description]" but not to "[Description] is [Name]". (3) We propose and verify the hypothesis that LLMs possess an inherent bias in fact recalling during knowledge application, which explains and underscores the importance of the document structure to successful learning. (4) The negative impact of this bias on the downstream performance of LLMs can hardly be mitigated through training alone. These findings offer a novel perspective on interpreting LLMs' generalization through their intrinsic mechanisms and provide insights for developing more effective learning methods. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/alibaba/thinking_bias.git.

papers.title: Hopping Too Late: Exploring the Limitations of Large Language Models on Multi-Hop Queries
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally compute answers to multi-hop queries, and why do they sometimes fail?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers a sequential latent reasoning pathway in LLMs for two-hop queries and introduces a novel 'back-patching' analysis method that can correct many previously incorrect answers.
papers.conclusion: LLMs use a sequential pathway for latent multi-hop reasoning, and the introduced back-patching method can improve performance, opening opportunities for understanding and improving such reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The bridge entity (first hop answer) is resolved in the early layers of the model.
The second hop is resolved in later layers, only after the first hop is resolved.
The sequential nature can cause failure if the later layers lack the necessary knowledge or functionality.
Back-patching (patching a later hidden representation back to an earlier layer) can correct up to 66% of previously incorrect cases.
Information about the bridge entity propagates from the first hop position to the last token position, primarily through middle layers.
papers.limitation:
The mechanistic methods used (e.g., Patchscopes, vocabulary projections) are approximations.
The study focuses on one prominent latent reasoning pathway, but others likely exist.
The work examines only two-hop queries, not more complex multi-step reasoning.
Back-patching is not a practical inference method without an efficient way to select source and target layers a priori.
future_direction: Expanding the analysis to queries with three or more hops and additional reasoning tasks.
Developing methods to efficiently select source and target layers for back-patching to make it a viable inference method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can solve complex multi-step problems, but little is known about how these computations are implemented internally. Motivated by this, we study how LLMs answer multi-hop queries such as "The spouse of the performer of Imagine is". These queries require two information extraction steps: a latent one for resolving the first hop ("the performer of Imagine") into the bridge entity (John Lennon), and another for resolving the second hop ("the spouse of John Lennon") into the target entity (Yoko Ono). Understanding how the latent step is computed internally is key to understanding the overall computation. By carefully analyzing the internal computations of transformer-based LLMs, we discover that the bridge entity is resolved in the early layers of the model. Then, only after this resolution, the two-hop query is solved in the later layers. Because the second hop commences in later layers, there could be cases where these layers no longer encode the necessary knowledge for correctly predicting the answer. Motivated by this, we propose a novel "back-patching" analysis method whereby a hidden representation from a later layer is patched back to an earlier layer. We find that in up to 66% of previously incorrect cases there exists a back-patch that results in the correct generation of the answer, showing that the later layers indeed sometimes lack the needed functionality. Overall, our methods and findings open further opportunities for understanding and improving latent reasoning in transformer-based LLMs.

papers.title: When classifying grammatical role, BERT doesn’t care about word order... except when it matters
papers.research_question: How do BERT and GPT-2 represent grammatical role, especially in non-prototypical sentences where word order is necessary for correct classification?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that word order is crucial for grammatical role representation in non-prototypical cases, with syntactic information gradually emerging in later layers of BERT and GPT-2, while early layers rely on lexical semantics.
papers.conclusion: Considering non-prototypical instances is crucial for understanding how language models represent syntactic information, as average probing can be misleading.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantics dominates early layer embeddings, while syntactic word order information is acquired in later layers for non-prototypical sentences.
Models can represent meaning based on syntactic word order, overriding lexical cues, as demonstrated with argument-swapped sentences.
Syntactic word order is significant beyond local coherence, as probes fail on locally shuffled sentences for non-prototypical cases.
papers.abstract: Because meaning can often be inferred from lexical semantics alone, word order is often a redundant cue in natural language. For example, the words chopped, chef, and onion are more likely used to convey "The chef chopped the onion," not "The onion chopped the chef." Recent work has shown large language models to be surprisingly word order invariant, but crucially has largely considered natural prototypical inputs, where compositional meaning mostly matches lexical expectations. To overcome this confound, we probe grammatical role representation in English BERT and GPT-2, on instances where lexical expectations are not sufficient, and word order knowledge is necessary for correct classification. Such nonprototypical instances are naturally occurring English sentences with inanimate subjects or animate objects, or sentences where we systematically swap the arguments to make sentences like "The onion chopped the chef". We find that, while early layer embeddings are largely lexical, word order is in fact crucial in defining the later-layer representations of words in semantically non-prototypical positions. Our experiments isolate the effect of word order on the contextualization process, and highlight how models use context in the uncommon, but critical, instances where it matters.

papers.title: Probing Latent Knowledge Conflict for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
papers.research_question: How can we improve contextual faithfulness in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems by moving beyond black-box interventions and analyzing the model's internal reasoning process? Specifically, how is conflict represented in the model's latent space and how does it disrupt faithful generation?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces ProbeRAG, a framework that leverages latent probing to detect knowledge conflicts in the model's hidden states and uses conflict-aware attention modulation to improve contextual faithfulness in RAG systems.
papers.conclusion: ProbeRAG effectively improves contextual faithfulness in RAG by moving beyond black-box interventions to internal guidance, demonstrating consistent and robust performance across various models and datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Conflicting and aligned knowledge states are linearly separable in the model's latent space, providing a detectable 'conflict feature'.
Contextual noise systematically increases the entropy of these representations, obscuring the conflict feature.
ProbeRAG, which integrates fine-grained knowledge pruning, latent conflict probing, and conflict-aware attention, substantially improves accuracy and contextual faithfulness across multiple benchmarks and models.
The accuracy of the conflict probe is positively correlated with the model's ability to generate faithful responses.
Attention visualization shows that after training with the attention-guidance loss, the model allocates more attention to tokens marked as conflicting knowledge.
papers.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a powerful paradigm to enhance the factuality of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing RAG systems often suffer from an unfaithfulness issue, where the model's response contradicts evidence from the retrieved context. Existing approaches to improving contextual faithfulness largely rely on external interventions, such as prompt engineering, decoding constraints, or reward-based fine-tuning. These works treat the LLM as a black box and overlook a crucial question: how does the LLM internally integrate retrieved evidence with its parametric memory, particularly under knowledge conflicts? To address this gap, we conduct a probing-based analysis of hidden-state representations in LLMs and observe three findings: knowledge integration occurs hierarchically, conflicts manifest as latent signals at the sentence level, and irrelevant context is often amplified when aligned with parametric knowledge. Building on these findings, we propose CLEAR (Conflict-Localized and Enhanced Attention for RAG), a framework that (i) decomposes context into fine-grained sentence-level knowledge, (ii) employs hidden-state probing to localize conflicting knowledge, and (iii) introduces conflict-aware fine-tuning to guide the model to accurately integrate retrieved evidence. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate that CLEAR substantially improves both accuracy and contextual faithfulness, consistently outperforming strong baselines under diverse conflict conditions. The related resources are available at https://github.com/LinfengGao/CLEAR.

papers.title: Constructing Efficient Fact-Storing MLPs for Transformers
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how MLP input and output geometries affect fact-storage capacity, how MLPs achieve parameter-efficient fact-storage, and how fact-storing MLPs interface with the rest of the Transformer stack.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an MLP construction framework for fact storage that improves over prior work in generality, efficiency, and usability, and uses it to gain insights into MLP fact-storage mechanisms.
papers.conclusion: By directly constructing MLPs to store facts, we provide a theoretical framework for studying fact storage and a path toward more robust fact manipulation in LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
They discover a metric ρ(V) on value embeddings that predicts fact-storage capacity for both constructed and gradient-descent-trained MLPs with R^2 > 97%.
They identify a simple encoder-decoder mechanism that empirically matches gradient-descent MLP facts-per-parameter asymptotics across all tested inputs and outputs.
They uncover a fundamental tradeoff between an MLP’s fact-storage capacity and its usability within Transformers.
They demonstrate modular fact editing on one-layer Transformers by replacing entire MLPs, doubling the fact-editing score of SoTA methods when editing 10% of the fact set.
Their construction requires 5–150× fewer parameters than prior constructions and matches information-theoretic bounds for some embeddings.
papers.abstract: The success of large language models (LLMs) can be attributed in part to their ability to efficiently store factual knowledge as key-value mappings within their MLP parameters. Recent work has proposed explicit weight constructions to build such fact-storing MLPs, providing an improved understanding of LLM fact storage mechanisms. In this paper, we introduce an MLP construction framework that improves over previous constructions in three areas: it 1) works for all but a measure-zero set of feasible input-output pairs, 2) achieves asymptotically optimal parameter efficiency matching information-theoretic bounds for some embeddings, and 3) maintains usability within Transformers for factual recall. Through our improvements, we 1) discover a metric on value embeddings that characterizes facts-per-parameter scaling for both constructed and gradient-descent-trained MLPs, 2) identify a simple encoder-decoder mechanism that empirically matches gradient-descent MLP facts-per-parameter asymptotics across all the inputs and outputs we test, and 3) uncover a fundamental tradeoff between an MLP's fact-storage capacity and its usability within Transformers. Finally, we demonstrate a proof-of-concept application of fact-storing MLPs: modular fact editing on one-layer Transformers by \textit{replacing entire MLPs at once}.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: Knowledge Graph Enhanced Large Language Model Editing
papers.research_question: How can model editing methods capture and incorporate changes in associated knowledge to improve the generalization ability of post-edit large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes GLAME, a novel model editing method that leverages knowledge graphs to capture associated knowledge changes and integrates them into the editing process, improving the generalization ability of post-edit LLMs.
papers.conclusion: GLAME effectively improves the generalization ability of post-edit LLMs by using knowledge graphs to capture and integrate associated knowledge changes during editing.
papers.key_findings:
GLAME outperforms state-of-the-art editing methods on multiple datasets, especially on Portability Score for multi-hop reasoning.
Simply adding external knowledge without the proposed graph-based edit module (as in ROME-KG and MEMIT-KG) degrades performance.
Ablation studies show the importance of the graph structure and the Graph-based Knowledge Edit (GKE) module.
Increasing the subgraph order improves performance up to a point, after which noise may be introduced.
The method is effective even when the subgraph only includes the direct edit triple (s, r, o*).
papers.limitation:
The framework's reliance on knowledge graphs may be constrained by the availability and quality of relevant knowledge.
The framework may be restricted in some unstructured edit scenarios, such as event-based knowledge editing or scenarios with no explicit association to the knowledge graph.
future_direction: Develop more sophisticated subgraph sampling strategies to enhance subgraph quality and more accurately capture knowledge changes.
Design more flexible strategies to identify key entities in edit samples and construct associated subgraphs, extending the method to more general editing scenarios.

papers.title: Is This the Subspace You Are Looking for? An Interpretability Illusion for Subspace Activation Patching
papers.research_question: Does the success of activation patching in finding interpretable subspaces reliably indicate that a subspace faithfully encodes a feature, or can it lead to misleading interpretability results?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that subspace activation patching can create an interpretability illusion where a subspace appears to encode a feature but actually works by activating a dormant, causally disconnected pathway, rather than faithfully representing the model's computation.
papers.conclusion: Subspace activation patching can be misleading, creating an illusion of interpretability. Successful patching alone is insufficient evidence that a subspace faithfully represents a feature; additional validation is required.
papers.key_findings:
A distilled mathematical example shows how patching along a sum of a causally disconnected and a dormant direction can create an illusory effect.
In the IOI task, a 1-dimensional subspace in an MLP layer (found via DAS) appears to encode position information, despite the layer being non-essential to the known circuit.
In factual recall, 1-dimensional activation patches are approximately equivalent to rank-1 model edits (ROME), providing a mechanistic explanation for why such edits can work even when the fact is not stored in the edited weights.
The illusion is argued to be prevalent due to the high-dimensional kernel of MLP down-projections and the linear separability of features in activation spaces.
papers.limitation: The illusion is demonstrated in specific tasks (IOI, factual recall) and a specific model (GPT-2 Small); its prevalence in other models and tasks requires further study.
future_direction: Develop methods to distinguish faithful subspaces from illusory ones.
Test the prevalence of the illusion in a wider range of models and tasks.
Explore the implications for other interpretability methods that rely on subspace interventions.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand model behaviors in terms of specific, interpretable features, often hypothesized to manifest as low-dimensional subspaces of activations. Specifically, recent studies have explored subspace interventions (such as activation patching) as a way to simultaneously manipulate model behavior and attribute the features behind it to given subspaces. In this work, we demonstrate that these two aims diverge, potentially leading to an illusory sense of interpretability. Counterintuitively, even if a subspace intervention makes the model's output behave as if the value of a feature was changed, this effect may be achieved by activating a dormant parallel pathway leveraging another subspace that is causally disconnected from model outputs. We demonstrate this phenomenon in a distilled mathematical example, in two real-world domains (the indirect object identification task and factual recall), and present evidence for its prevalence in practice. In the context of factual recall, we further show a link to rank-1 fact editing, providing a mechanistic explanation for previous work observing an inconsistency between fact editing performance and fact localization. However, this does not imply that activation patching of subspaces is intrinsically unfit for interpretability. To contextualize our findings, we also show what a success case looks like in a task (indirect object identification) where prior manual circuit analysis informs an understanding of the location of a feature. We explore the additional evidence needed to argue that a patched subspace is faithful.

papers.title: Probing Linguistic Information for Logical Inference in Pre-trained Language Models
papers.research_question: Do pre-trained language models encode linguistic information essential to symbolic inference systems? Do they acquire new linguistic information for inference during fine-tuning for the NLI task?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a probing methodology to assess linguistic information for logical inference in pre-trained language models, finding that they encode some but not all types of information, and that fine-tuning can help acquire missing information.
papers.conclusion: Pre-trained language models encode some linguistic information for inference, with more on simple than complex phenomena, and can acquire additional information through fine-tuning, showing potential as knowledge bases for symbolic reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-trained language models encode more information on simple semantic phenomena (e.g., lexical alignment, contradiction signatures) than on complex phenomena (e.g., monotonicity, sentiment and relational knowledge alignment).
Linear classifiers may misinterpret semantic information, while MLP classifiers achieve higher accuracy and similar selectivity, suggesting that more expressive probes are needed for semantic tasks.
Label-wise analysis shows that the amount of linguistic information encoded varies across labels, with models performing better on some labels than others.
Pre-trained language models can learn some missing linguistic information (e.g., for sentiment and relational-knowledge alignment) through fine-tuning on NLI data, but not for monotonicity.
Pre-trained language models encode significantly more linguistic information for inference than baseline word embeddings, as measured by information gain.
papers.limitation:
Even high expressive classifiers like MLP fail to perform well on tasks with monotonicity and higher-level semantic reasoning.
The training data of MultiNLI may not contain enough examples about monotonicity, which could explain why fine-tuning does not improve performance on monotonicity polarization.
future_direction: Conduct further analysis on each type of linguistic information in language models by constructing more detailed probing datasets.
Design logical systems that can access linguistic information from pre-trained language models and apply them in the inference process for improved performance on large benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Progress in pre-trained language models has led to a surge of impressive results on downstream tasks for natural language understanding. Recent work on probing pre-trained language models uncovered a wide range of linguistic properties encoded in their contextualized representations. However, it is unclear whether they encode semantic knowledge that is crucial to symbolic inference methods. We propose a methodology for probing knowledge for inference that logical systems require but often lack in pre-trained language model representations. Our probing datasets cover a list of key types of knowledge used by many symbolic inference systems. We find that (i) pre-trained language models do encode several types of knowledge for inference, but there are also some types of knowledge for inference that are not encoded, (ii) language models can effectively learn missing knowledge for inference through fine-tuning. Overall, our findings provide insights into which aspects of knowledge for inference language models and their pre-training procedures capture. Moreover, we have demonstrated language models' potential as semantic and background knowledge bases for supporting symbolic inference methods.

papers.title: RelEdit: Evaluating Conceptual Knowledge Editing in Language Models via Relational Reasoning
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the impact of conceptual knowledge editing on a model's related beliefs and relational reasoning abilities?
